depth_zones.hadal: Working design band: deeper than roughly 6,000 m

note: Broad design conventions, not exact species ranges. Recipes do not yet drive the live game. Check each taxon and site before population.

habitats.name: Coral terraces
habitats.look: Branching fans rise above rough stone. Small animals occupy branches, ledges and crevices; bare rock remains visible between colonies.
habitats.terrain: Layered hard outcrops with sheltered pockets and exposed crests.
habitats.movement: Flexible branches respond gently to current; drifting food particles show flow direction.
habitats.arrival: A few isolated fans appear first. Around a ridge, the silhouettes become a layered garden.
habitats.scenario: Follow the current to document animals sheltering on a coral colony.
habitats.research: Study suspension feeding and cooperative habitat structure; proposed village filtration research.
rules: Require hard substrate and sufficient food/current.
Cluster colonies; vary height, spacing and orientation.
Exclude the hot center of active vents.
variations: Sparse crest becoming a dense terrace
habitats.reference: Papahānaumokuākea expedition coral-and-sponge community; exact image depth not verified.
habitats.certainty: Representative habitat, not a measured reconstruction.

habitats.name: Sponge gardens
habitats.look: Pale cups and irregular sponge forms stand against a low rocky platform. The colony has open gaps, overhangs and contrasting textures.
habitats.terrain: Carbonate ledges and hard patches, with sediment between them.
habitats.movement: Subtle current-driven particles; animals moving between stationary structures.
habitats.arrival: Low cups and scattered forms gradually resolve into a garden across the platform.
habitats.scenario: Compare organisms at exposed and sheltered edges of a colony.
habitats.research: Explore sponge-associated microbial partnerships; potential filtration concepts are fictional upgrades.
rules: Use hard attachment points.
Allow mixed coral/sponge patches.
Choose actual sponge species only after depth and region verification.
habitats.reference: NOAA 2021 North Atlantic Stepping Stones, Dive 08 carbonate platform.
habitats.certainty: An example site, not the appearance of every sponge habitat.

habitats.name: Canyon walls
habitats.look: A wall fills the view. Bedding, cracks and undercuts create stacked shelters; attached life uses suitable exposed surfaces.
habitats.terrain: Walls, terraces, eroded pockets and talus below the cliff.
habitats.movement: Cross-flow around ledges; localized sediment plumes near the bottom.
habitats.arrival: The floor slopes, scattered blocks increase, then a wall rises into the headlamp beam.
habitats.scenario: Search successive ledges and look beneath overhangs for sheltered life.
habitats.research: Compare attachment and shelter strategies; proposed habitat engineering research.
rules: Place attached animals using surface normals, including walls.
Keep swim routes around ledges.
Separate geological layers from biological colonies.
habitats.reference: NOAA East of Veatch Canyon image, Exploring Atlantic Canyons and Seamounts 2014.
habitats.certainty: Do not infer species or brooding behavior for every generated alcove.

habitats.name: Hydrothermal vent fields
habitats.look: Dark mineral towers, turbulent mineral-laden fluid and dense animal patches. Life concentrates around suitable mixed waters rather than filling every surface.
habitats.terrain: Fractured volcanic substrate, chimneys and mineral aprons.
habitats.movement: Rising fluid bends with the ambient current; shimmering flow and moving animals define the scene.
habitats.arrival: Fractures and mineral staining lead to diffuse flow, then the towers appear through suspended particles.
habitats.scenario: Compare a cool mixing zone with a hotter vent outlet using instruments.
habitats.research: Microbial heat/chemical adaptations; engineered bioreactor concepts remain game fiction.
rules: Require hydrothermal circulation in suitable geology.
Mix hot outlet fluid into cold surrounding water.
Use province-appropriate species; this Marianas image does not document Riftia.
variations: Diffuse-flow apron beside an inactive tower
habitats.reference: NOAA 2016 Deepwater Exploration of the Marianas: active chimney with vent animals.
habitats.certainty: Black smoke is suspended minerals, not combustion or a universal gas-bubble effect.

habitats.name: Cold seeps
habitats.look: Mussel beds gather under a carbonate ledge, with patchy microbial cover and sediment around them. Bubble streams occur at some seeps, not all.
habitats.terrain: Sediment, carbonate crusts, cracks and overhangs.
habitats.movement: Where documented, escaping gas bubbles rise from small sources; other seeps appear visually quiet.
habitats.arrival: An isolated shell patch leads to carbonate slabs, then a living bed beneath an overhang.
habitats.scenario: Trace a chemical gradient and compare a living mussel bed with empty shells.
habitats.research: Methane- and sulfur-associated symbioses; proposed chemical-sensing technology.
rules: Require a localized fluid/chemical source.
Tie animals to gradients and attachment surfaces.
Keep hydrate and bubbles conditional on local conditions.
variations: Bubbling seep among mixed attached life
habitats.reference: NOAA Bathymodiolus mussels beneath carbonate; secondary image shows an Alaska bubbling seep.
habitats.certainty: Hydrate presence in the reference is not a rule for all seeps.

habitats.name: Brine-pool margins
habitats.look: A distinct pool-like surface sits within the seabed. The reference pool is small; surrounding terrain is as important as the liquid boundary.
life: Site-dependent mussels or other margin fauna
habitats.terrain: A depression linked to saline fluid sources, with a distinct rim.
habitats.movement: Density-interface ripples and refraction; avoid treating it as an air-filled lake.
habitats.arrival: Sediment changes around a depression and a reflective-looking boundary resolves at close range.
habitats.scenario: Sample along the edge while comparing salinity and oxygen readings.
habitats.research: Salt-adaptation research candidates; village applications require a documented organism.
rules: Require suitable salt-bearing geology and brine supply.
Constrain pools to depressions.
Do not fill anoxic brine with ordinary fish and corals.
habitats.reference: NOAA Gulf of Mexico, 19 April 2018: 1.2 m pool at 1,067 m depth.
habitats.certainty: Pool size, salinity, toxicity and rim communities vary; this is not a hadal reference.

habitats.name: Abyssal nodule fields
habitats.look: Small dark nodules interrupt fine sediment. Repeated small forms create texture; trails, burrows and isolated animals provide discoveries rather than a continuous forest.
life: Sea cucumbers and brittle stars at suitable sites
habitats.terrain: Broad sediment expanses with varying nodule cover and occasional exposed rock.
habitats.movement: Slow benthic activity and drifting marine snow; background density stays modest.
habitats.arrival: Rock relief diminishes, sediment opens out and scattered nodules gradually become a field.
habitats.scenario: Use the scanner to discover small life attached to hard nodules.
habitats.research: Explore attachment and slow-growth strategies; proposed gentle sampling tools.
rules: Keep background animal abundance lower than biological hotspots.
Vary nodule size and coverage with coherent patches.
Do not imply nodules regenerate on a gameplay timescale.
habitats.reference: NOAA 2026 Cook Islands ROV Exploration, Dive 08: nodule-covered seamount substrate, starting depth 3,700 m.
habitats.certainty: This photograph is seamount substrate, not proof of a flat plain. Not all abyssal seabeds contain nodules or share this density.

habitats.name: Whale-fall discoveries
habitats.look: A large skeleton forms a recognizable focal point on sediment. The carcass or bones support different communities as the fall ages.
life: Bone-associated worms such as Osedax where documented
habitats.terrain: A local food-fall patch placed over an otherwise eligible seabed.
habitats.movement: Concentrated local activity around food and shelter; not constant uniform swarms.
habitats.arrival: Scattered bones or scavengers draw attention before the main skeleton enters the beam.
habitats.scenario: Document a chosen stage of decomposition and the organisms using it.
habitats.research: Study nutrient recycling and symbioses; proposed waste-processing research.
rules: Treat as a rare encounter overlay, not a continent-sized biome.
Choose one persistent stage when generating.
Avoid bait-camera abundance as a background-density target.
habitats.reference: NOAA Undersea Research Program gray-whale skeleton photograph, 2004; low resolution.
habitats.certainty: The photograph illustrates a skeletal stage, not all stages simultaneously.

habitats.name: Hadal trench mosaics
habitats.look: The Java Trench figure shows both fine sediment and rougher slopes. The trench is a mosaic of terrain, not an endless vertical crack or a universal lush reef.
habitats.terrain: Fine sediment on flatter floors; bedrock and debris on steeper sections.
habitats.movement: Sparse local animal movement and instrument-led discoveries.
habitats.arrival: The route descends through progressively changing substrate and relief, with suitable depth-specific life.
habitats.scenario: Survey a sediment pocket and nearby rock exposure while monitoring pressure.
habitats.research: Pressure adaptation; fictional high-pressure lab upgrades need documented species evidence.
rules: Reserve for a genuine deeper progression band.
Use pressure/depth checks independently of geology.
Potential chemosynthetic deposits in the study remain a hypothesis, not confirmed vents.
habitats.reference: Jamieson et al. 2022, Figure 4; Java Trench observations including 5,760–7,168 m panels.
habitats.certainty: One trench study; it cannot stand for every trench or the deepest point in every ocean.
